name: Jade Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead installer at Brightline, a small firm of about twelve people that does solar panels, heat pumps, battery storage and ordinary house wiring. A normal day starts at the warehouse at half seven, loading the van with inverters and cable, then I'm on a roof or in a loft until four with Kofi (my second electrician). I like that the work feels useful, like we're actually fixing something bigger than one house. What wears me out is customers who've read one article online and want to argue about panel angles.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in renewables rather than general wiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did general wiring for six years, then Brightline needed someone with a master's licence who could do the battery and switchboard side. I'm one of the few women in the trade around here, and I'm good, so I got the job. My partner Priya teaches primary school, and we rent a small terraced house. We've got about three months of bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the real story was never AI, it was the energy switch. Every house needs rewiring for heat pumps and car chargers, and that's not going anywhere. I'd probably post something like that on the trade group I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. My work is ninety percent hands and judgement. I do use a chatbot now and then to draft quotes, and that would carry on saving me twenty minutes a day, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going at Brightline. I want to get my battery storage certificate next spring, which the firm would pay half of. And Priya and I would keep saving towards a deposit, maybe two hundred a month more if the rent doesn't jump again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because all the noise was for nothing, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned rent jumping. How much is that on your mind in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a lot, actually. Our landlord put it up nine percent last year. That's the thing that makes me check my bank app, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Brightline you'd worry about even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe Lucy in the office, if the quoting software gets better, but she does so much more than quotes. In this picture everyone stays.

say: I'd say the real story is the **energy switch**, not AI.
I'd post that every house needs **rewiring** for heat pumps and chargers.
think: My work is mostly **hands and judgement**, so AI barely touches it.
The thing that worries me is **rent**, which went up nine percent.
do: Get my **battery storage certificate** next spring with Brightline paying half.
Save an extra **two hundred a month** towards a deposit with Priya.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat after all the noise.
S0.quote: Every house needs rewiring for heat pumps and car chargers, and that's not going anywhere.
fieldNote: She frames her trade around the **energy transition**, which gives her confidence.
Her real pressure is **rent**, not technology.
She already uses a chatbot lightly, which fits her **steady** stance on tools.

steps.text: Take the battery storage course next spring with Brightline paying half
Add two hundred a month to the house deposit with Priya
Carry on leading solar and heat pump installs at Brightline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on how firms use it, so the time it saves goes to workers and not just the owners. I'd say it at the union meeting, and I'd probably say it to Mark (the owner of Brightline) too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my hands are fine for now, but the office will change. Quotes, ordering, booking jobs, all of that goes to software. That's Lucy's whole job, and it's a chunk of mine too, because I do the site surveys and write them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the quoting and design software properly once I saw it work on a couple of real jobs, not before. I'd ask Mark to keep Lucy and move her into customer follow-ups. And I'd join the electricians' union properly; I've been meaning to for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My job's safe, but I can feel the floor tilting under the people around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What exactly would change in your own week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The survey write-ups. Right now I spend Friday afternoons typing up loft measurements and photos into a report. If software does that from my photos, I get Friday back, which is lovely, or Mark books me another install, which is less lovely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy (our office coordinator at Brightline) first. She's fifty-three, she's brilliant with angry customers, and she'd find it hard to get another office job if software does quotes and bookings.

say: I'd say the time AI saves should go to **workers**, not just owners.
I'd tell Mark (Brightline's owner) to **keep Lucy** and move her into follow-ups.
think: My hands are safe, but the **office side** is going to software.
My Friday **survey write-ups** would probably disappear, for better or worse.
do: Learn the **quoting software** after seeing it work on real jobs.
Ask Mark to move Lucy into **customer follow-ups**.
Join the **electricians' union** properly this year.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching the floor tilt under the people around her.
S1.quote: My job's safe, but I can feel the floor tilting under the people around me.
fieldNote: She separates her own safety from **colleagues' risk** very clearly.
Her steady style shows in wanting to see software **proven on real jobs** first.
Losing Friday paperwork could mean **more installs**, not more free time.

steps.text: Learn Brightline's new quoting software after two real test jobs
Ask Mark to move Lucy into customer follow-ups
Join the electricians' union before the end of the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments have to step in now: paid retraining, public works, maybe a tax on firms that replace workers with machines. I'd be loud about it online and at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years to the AI and five to the robots puts me at thirty-two. The roof work goes last because roofs are awkward, but new builds with prefab wiring could go fast. I don't think my licence would protect me as much as I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the three years before the robots to move toward inspection and grid connection work, where you need a person signing off. I'd start the inspector course straight away and use the AI tools to study. Priya and I would put the deposit on hold and keep it as a cushion instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got some control, but not much time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between thinking AI and robots mean for your day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the surveys, quotes and design all go to software, so I'm just the hands. Then by 2031 the hands go too. So I've got three years where I'm basically a skilled pair of arms, and I need to use them to get somewhere a robot can't sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Priya (your partner) talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job's safer than mine, honestly. Teachers might be all right longer because parents want a person. We'd probably agree she's the steady income and I'm the one who has to move.

say: I'd call for **paid retraining** and public works straight away.
I'd back a **tax on firms** that replace workers with machines.
think: By **2031** prefab new builds could need far fewer electricians.
My **licence** may not protect me as much as I'd like.
do: Start the **inspector course** immediately and use AI tools to study.
Move towards **grid connection** work that needs a human signature.
Hold the house **deposit** as a cushion instead of buying.
feel: **Anxious**, with some control but very little time.
S2.quote: I've got three years where I'm basically a skilled pair of arms, and I need to use them to get somewhere a robot can't sign.
fieldNote: She reads the **three-year gap** precisely and plans around it.
She expects Priya's **teaching job** to be the household's steady income.
Her politics and plans line up: public support plus her own **retraining**.

steps.text: Enrol in the electrical inspector course within the first month
Use AI tools to study wiring regulations for the inspector exam
Keep the house deposit as a cushion instead of buying
Campaign online and at the union for paid retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time if we start now, so start now. I'd push the union to get training budgets agreed with the big contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years to the AI and eight to the robots means I'd be thirty-five when the hands-on side goes. That's a decent run. But I'd want to be an inspector or a grid engineer by then, not still on roofs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the battery certificate and start the inspector course part-time. I'd use the design software at Brightline as soon as it's reliable. Priya and I might still buy, but somewhere cheaper, so we're not stretched if I take a pay cut while switching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more the busy kind. I like having a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might take a pay cut. How much could you handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe ten percent for a year or two. Inspector jobs start lower than senior installer pay. With Priya's salary and three months saved, we could ride that out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a young woman thinking of starting an apprenticeship in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say do it, but plan to move off the tools by your mid-thirties. Learn the regulations, the testing and the paperwork side too, because a robot can pull cable but someone still has to be responsible.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if we start now.
I'd push the union for **training budgets** with the big contractors.
think: I'd be **thirty-five** when the hands-on side goes, which is a decent run.
I want to be an **inspector** or grid engineer by then.
do: Finish the **battery certificate** and start the inspector course part-time.
Use Brightline's **design software** once it's reliable.
Buy somewhere **cheaper** to survive a pay cut during the switch.
feel: **Anxious**, but the busy kind that likes a list.
S3.quote: A robot can pull cable but someone still has to be responsible.
fieldNote: She accepts a **ten percent pay cut** as the cost of switching.
She advises young women to plan to **leave the tools** by their mid-thirties.
Her anxiety turns into **planning** when there's time.

steps.text: Start the inspector course part-time while still installing
Use Brightline's design software once it works reliably
Buy a cheaper house that survives a ten percent pay cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to do this fairly, with training paid for and nobody thrown out overnight. That's what I'd keep saying at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, ten years to the AI and thirteen to the robots means I'm forty before my hands matter less. I'd have time to become an inspector, maybe even teach at the college. I'd be fine. I'd worry more about the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep installing for now and buy the house with Priya. Over a few years I'd add the inspector qualification and maybe teach evening classes at the college. I'd start using the AI tools more as they get good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the back of my mind. It's like a storm forecast for next season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change whether you'd have children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. We'd want to wait a few years anyway. If anything, ten years makes it feel more possible, because I'd know where I'm heading by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about the apprentices?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd be qualifying around 2030 into a trade that changes in 2039. Kofi (my second electrician at Brightline) is twenty-two. He'd have nine good years and then have to start again.

say: I'd say ten years is a chance to do this **fairly**.
I'd push for **paid training** so nobody gets thrown out overnight.
think: I'd be **forty** before my hands matter less.
The **apprentices** coming through now have far more to lose than I do.
do: Buy the **house** with Priya in the next couple of years.
Add the **inspector qualification** over a few years.
Teach **evening classes** at the college later on.
feel: **Uneasy** in the background, like a storm forecast for next season.
S4.quote: Kofi (my second electrician at Brightline) is twenty-two. He'd have nine good years and then have to start again.
fieldNote: With a decade she feels secure and shifts worry to **younger workers**.
Teaching at the college appeals as a long-term **human role**.
Her family plans stay **on track** with more warning.

steps.text: Buy a house with Priya within the next two years
Add the electrical inspector qualification over the next few years
Keep leading installs at Brightline in the meantime

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years for the office side and five for the robots doesn't give anyone, including the government, time to put proper support in place. What would help is retraining that's actually paid, so you're not choosing between rent and a course, and public money going into grid and insulation work that keeps people like me busy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about women in the trade. It took me years to be taken seriously on site. If robots take over the hands-on work, the industry could easily go back to a few men in an office supervising machines, and we'd lose the ground we fought for. I spent years earning respect on building sites as a woman electrician. I'm not handing that over to a robot without a fight.

headlineQuote: I spent years earning respect on building sites as a woman electrician. I'm not handing that over to a robot without a fight.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old lead installer** at a small solar and heat pump firm, renting with her partner Priya.
She's **progressive** and practical, trusting public investment and unions more than tech firms.
She uses AI tools **now and then** and would learn more once she saw them work on real jobs.
Her worry grows with each AGI picture, and she'd use extra time to move into **grid and inspection** work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time for paid retraining or public support to catch up.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** so she doesn't have to choose between rent and a course.
**Public money** for grid and insulation work that keeps electricians busy.
